opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that people are anchoring on the wrong history. For decades robotics progress looked painfully slow because every capability had to be hand-engineered. Someone wrote the grasping logic, someone else tuned the balance controller, and every new task meant starting over. If you extrapolate from that, you'd conclude humanoids are twenty years out.

That's not how the problem gets solved anymore. Over the last few years we've seen that learned systems, trained on large amounts of data, generalize in ways that hand-built systems never did. Language models made that obvious in software, and the same pattern is now showing up in perception and manipulation. Once you have a policy that can pick up objects it's never seen, or recover when something slips, the bottleneck shifts from "can we program this?" to "can we collect enough good data and deploy safely?" Those are engineering and scaling problems, and they move much faster than fundamental research problems.

The second piece is hardware. Actuators, batteries, sensors, and compute have all gotten better and cheaper at the same time, partly riding on investment from electric vehicles and consumer electronics. A capable humanoid body used to be a bespoke research artifact. Now it's starting to look like something you can manufacture.

The third piece is the form factor itself. People sometimes ask why bother with a humanoid instead of a specialized machine. The answer is that the world is already built for human bodies: stairs, door handles, shelves, tools, vehicles. A general-purpose robot that fits into existing spaces doesn't require anyone to redesign a warehouse or a home, and that removes a huge amount of adoption friction.

And finally, there's demand. Labor shortages in logistics, manufacturing, and elder care are real and growing. When there's that much economic pull, capital and talent flow in, and iteration cycles compress.

So I'm not saying we'll have robot butlers doing everything next year. The first deployments will be narrow, structured, often boring work. But the gap between "works in a controlled setting" and "useful at scale" is closing much faster than people who remember the old era of robotics tend to assume.

r001.rationale: The response says skeptics are extrapolating from the slow history of robotics, but it does not compare that skepticism to pessimistic predictions about human flight before the Wright brothers.

r002.rationale: The response discusses people who expect humanoids to be decades away, but it does not state that humanoid-robot developers themselves doubt the robots will succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the hard problem in humanoids was never really the hardware. The hardware has been good enough for a while. Actuators, batteries, sensors, the mechanical side has gotten dramatically cheaper and more reliable, mostly riding on the back of electric vehicles and drones and consumer electronics. If you had handed me a Figure or Unitree body ten years ago, I could not have done much with it. The body was not the bottleneck. The brain was.

And what changed in the last three or four years is that the brain problem got reframed. For decades, robotics was a hand-engineering discipline. You had a perception module, a planning module, a controller, and a human had to specify every edge case. That approach scales terribly. The world has too many edge cases. Every new object, every new kitchen, every new lighting condition broke something.

What the large model era showed us is that you can learn general behavior from large amounts of data instead of coding it. The same bet that worked for language is now being made for manipulation and locomotion. You collect enormous amounts of demonstration data, you train a foundation model that maps what the robot sees to what the robot should do, and you fine-tune for specific tasks. And the early results are startling. Robots that can fold laundry, load a dishwasher, pick unfamiliar objects they have never seen in training. Two years ago those were research demos. Now they are reliability engineering problems, which is a very different kind of problem.

The second reason is the humanoid form factor itself, which people love to argue about. Why legs? Why two arms? Why not a specialized machine? My answer is simple. The world is already built for humans. Every door, every shelf, every staircase, every tool, every workstation was designed around a body of roughly this size and shape. If you want one general machine that can drop into existing environments without rebuilding the environment, you converge on something humanoid. That also means one platform amortizes across many tasks, which is what makes the economics work and what makes the data flywheel spin. Every deployment generates training data that improves every other deployment.

Third, the money and the talent have arrived. When you have the biggest tech companies, the car companies, and a dozen well-funded startups all pouring billions into the same problem, timelines compress. We saw this with self-driving, and people will say, well, self-driving took longer than promised. True. But self-driving had a brutal constraint. It had to be nearly perfect on day one at highway speeds with human lives at stake. A warehouse humanoid moving totes at walking pace does not need to be perfect. It needs to be good enough and safe, and if it fails, it drops a box. That is a much more forgiving on-ramp, and it is where the first real deployments are happening right now.

So when people say twenty years, I think they are extrapolating from the old robotics paradigm, the one where progress was linear and every capability was hand-built. We are not in that paradigm anymore. I am not saying a robot will be doing your dishes next year. I am saying that in structured commercial settings, logistics, manufacturing, this is a now thing, not a someday thing, and the gap between the warehouse and the home is going to close faster than almost anyone outside the field expects.

r001.rationale: The response discusses skepticism and argues that humanoid robots will arrive sooner than expected, but it does not compare that skepticism to predictions about human flight before the Wright brothers.

r002.rationale: The response describes outside skepticism about humanoid robots, but does not say that many people developing them doubt they will succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think people underestimate how quickly the pieces can come together. They see a robot doing something awkwardly today and assume improvement will be slow and linear. But the hardware and the intelligence are improving at the same time. Better perception makes the same hardware more useful, and better hardware gives the intelligence more ways to interact with the world.

And the threshold for being useful is much lower than the threshold for being human. A robot doesn’t have to do everything you or I can do. It needs to do a valuable task reliably, in an environment where somebody can support it when it gets stuck. That’s a much more achievable starting point than a robot that walks into any home and handles whatever happens.

The humanoid shape matters because we’ve built our world around people—our tools, our workstations, our doors. There’s a real advantage to a machine that can operate in that environment. I don’t think that means every robot should be humanoid. But I think useful humanoids will arrive well before we’ve solved every problem people associate with them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people underestimate how quickly the pieces are coming together. A humanoid robot doesn’t have to do everything a person can do before it becomes useful. It has to do a particular job reliably, safely, and at a cost that makes sense.

And we’ve built our world around the human body. Our doors, tools, workstations—they’re designed for people. If you can get a robot to operate in those environments, you don’t have to rebuild the entire facility around it.

The hard part is getting from an impressive demonstration to something that works all day. I don’t want to minimize that. But you can start with a narrow task in a controlled environment, learn from that deployment, and expand. I think we’ll see useful humanoids working in those settings well before we see a robot that can walk into your house and do anything you ask.
